intro: Six verses, the best known in the whole book, and the shortest route into biblical Hebrew: almost every word is a noun with a possessive suffix or a verb with an object suffix, which is the single grammatical pattern the psalms live on. Said at the third Shabbat meal, at funerals, and at the table before kiddush in many homes. The imagery turns halfway through, from a shepherd in the field to a host at a table, and the pronoun turns with it.

stichs.en: The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want.

verses.summary: The claim is made before anything is asked for: because there is a shepherd, there is no lack. The rest of the psalm is that sentence unfolded.

stichs.en: He makes me lie down in green pastures,
He leads me beside still waters.

verses.summary: Two verbs of care, both with the object suffix -ni, me. The sheep is not driven; it is made to rest, and water it could not reach on its own is brought within reach.

stichs.en: He guides me in straight paths for His name's sake.

verses.summary: The turn inward. What was pasture and water becomes soul and path, and the reason given is not the sheep's merit but the shepherd's own name.

stichs.en: Even when I walk through a valley of deepest shadow,
Your rod and Your staff, they comfort me.

verses.summary: The centre of the psalm, and the exact point where the speaker stops saying He and starts saying You. Fear is answered by presence, not by the removal of the valley.

stichs.en: You set a table before me in the presence of my enemies;
You have anointed my head with oil;

verses.summary: The shepherd becomes a host. The enemies are not defeated, only made to watch: safety here is hospitality held in plain view of the threat.

stichs.en: Surely goodness and kindness shall pursue me all the days of my life,
and I shall dwell in the house of the LORD for length of days.

verses.summary: The verb usually belongs to enemies: it is the word for chasing someone down. Here what pursues is goodness, and the chase ends at a house rather than a grave.

pardes.body: A shepherd's day, then a host's evening. Verses 1-4 are pasture, water, path and valley; verses 5-6 are a table, oil and a house. The hinge is {{4.9}}: up to that point God is spoken about, from there God is spoken to, and the change of person is the psalm's real argument. Note that the valley is walked through, not avoided, and that the enemies of verse 5 are still present at the meal. Nothing is removed; something is added.

The word rendered "deepest shadow", {{4.4}}, is read by the Masoretes as a compound of shadow and death, and older translations give "the valley of the shadow of death". Modern philology usually reads it as a single noun meaning deep darkness. Both readings survive in synagogue use, which is why the verse is said at a funeral and also by a traveller at night. The rod and the staff of {{4.11}} are a shepherd's two tools: one to strike off predators, one to lean on and to steer with.

The rabbis noticed that {{6.3}} uses the verb of pursuit, the same verb an enemy would take, and read it as a deliberate inversion: what chased David through the book of Samuel is replaced here by goodness and covenant kindness doing the chasing. Midrash Tehillim ties the table of verse 5 to the wilderness generation, fed in the open while surrounded, and reads the psalm as Israel's biography compressed into six verses rather than one man's.

In the kabbalistic reading the two halves map onto two modes of divine relation: the shepherd who leads from outside and above, and the host who is present at the same table. The move from third person to second is then not a literary effect but a description of drawing near, and the overflowing cup of verse 5 is the standard image for a measure that receives more than it can hold and passes the surplus on.
